utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have document 1D04-0461 again, please. And I'd like -- I think it's page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You told us that, The mood at lunch today was normal, and you told us you can't remember the conversation, particularly you can't remember the conversation between Generals Gvero and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 21, please, of the English and B/C/S -- sorry, Serbian versions of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There it indicates: "We were with Generals Mladic, Perisic, and Gvero at the picnic table for a couple of hours. As I stated in my previous statement, Generals Gvero and Mladic were discussing the liberation of Srebrenica at lunch. They did not spend much time on it. General Perisic was present to hear this conversation. There were no signs of disagreement between the generals. There was a lot of joking around at lunch." Does that refresh your memory, sir, as to the conversation that took place at lunch?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a discussion of the liberation, because the General Mladic addressed it as you saw on the video-tape before, and that was in that same manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, in the video-tape he'd been expressing -- or indicating that there had been a victory at Srebrenica. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you recall anything else that was being said?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that yesterday discussion, and I believe it was this morning as well, so you heard the discussion. You want me to repeat what we -- what we heard, or what that part -- I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what -- you told us that there was a discussion of the liberation. Do you recall what General Perisic's reaction was to that discussion, if any?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it. He -- that he made some discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just not a hundred per cent understanding your answer, sir. You said, "I don't recall it. He -- that he made some discussion about it." Are you saying you don't recall what he said, or you don't believe he discussed it?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what he discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you spend the entire day of the 18th at Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we left in afternoon for Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you say "we left," who left?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group of Canadians that was listening, which I meant Mr. Zarubin, and Mrs. Zarubin, Mr. Lesic, and Mr. Ilija Rakanovic, and Ranko Rakanovic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how were you travel to Pale?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall who left first, the contingent of Canadians or General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I think he did -- left before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Perisic left before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If I could refresh your memory from paragraph 22 of the statement that's before you where it indicates: "After lunch I left for Pale with the other Canadians. We left before General Perisic." Does that assist you in refreshing your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are refreshing, but still, like I said, this is 14 years ago. I -- I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any reason why in September you'd sign a statement saying you left before General Perisic and today you wouldn't be sure?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, same thing. At that time, I -- I made the same statement as I said today, and I -- but you wrote it down, and I believe to me that didn't matter that much, was it we left before or he left before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So you're saying that the statement you reviewed and signed and made corrections to before signing doesn't actually reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Why would you sign it then, sir?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I didn't realise this was of that importance. I made a statement. I was there, and I -- and that I left, and I thought that was the main reason and most important.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. You were giving a statement to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor and a Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer. Is it your evidence that you didn't think it was important to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not be accurate for that time. I told you even then, and I'm saying the same thing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, we'll move on from here. Do you recall where General Mladic and Gvero were when you left Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were in Crna Rijeka. I -- I think they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go back to the video-tape we've been watching, sir, and we're going to start it at the -- restart it at the 51 minute and 53 second mark. And this footage is about 15 minutes long. It goes to 1 minute and -- sorry, 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 27 seconds. And I may -- I may stop once in a while during the footage to ask some questions. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I've stopped the tape at 52 minutes and 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you identify the two gentlemen seated at the table?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. President Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Paused again at 53 minutes and 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you identify the person in the colourful shirt closest to the camera?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranko Rakanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the gentleman next to him with the glasses?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ned Krayishnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You can see the head of somebody next to you. Are you able to recognise who that was?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am assuming this was Mrs. Zarubin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And on the other side of the person you think is Mrs. Zarubin?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zarubin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sir, do you recognise -- sir, do you recognise the voice of the person who is speaking now?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how does the volume of his voice on this tape compare with the volume of the other speakers we've heard so far? Do you need to hear a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I here him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, just -- would you -- I'm going to play a little bit more, and could you continue to listen, paying attention to the volume at which he is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, and for the record, I stopped at 1 hour, 6 minutes, and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could pause again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on how the volume of his voice compares to the other speakers?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was only closer to the video that his voice was much more clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Who was operating the video?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you see -- have you seen Mr. Lesic at all in this video up to this point in time?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't remember seeing him yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Would you pay attention to see if you do?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could continue, please, at 1:06:48.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I've stopped the tape at 1 hour, 10 minutes, and 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you just tell us where the segment that we've just watched, where that was?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pale. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. And I'm just going to ask that we play the next -- the next two minutes of the tape, from -- starting again from 1 hour, 10 minutes, and 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paused at 1 minute -- 1 hour, 10 minutes, and 35 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are we in the same room as we were in for the previous footage or have we changed locations?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe we are in same room.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll play it through to the end, and we'll come back to this issue. I just forgot to ask with the footage that we have been dealing with, with Mr. Krajisnik, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Radovan Karadzic in Pale, the date stamp on the video had said July 18th, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately what time of day that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And how long does it take to drive from Crna Rijeka to Pale?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never was timing, but I -- roughly would take 45 minutes or one hour, depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Pausing at 1 hour, 10 minutes, 58 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Not the greatest video, but the gentleman on the far right of the photo with the white shirt, who is that?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And the gentleman next to him, can you identify him?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranko Rakanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us who the person to his right is?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looks like it -- myself, but I'm not sure. I cannot see clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll just continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not -- it is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Pausing again at 1 minute, 11 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You just -- so it's not lost on the record, that person was not you, you said.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: 1 hour, 11 minutes, 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise either of the people seated at the head of the table?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And we've stopped the video at 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell -- or do you remember if you were present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this, I don't think I was present at this meeting, and I think this was in -- in Gorazde, little town which I cannot recall, that Mr. Rakanovic brothers and Milan Lesic went, and I believe I went to -- I had a cousin in Pale. I went to visit them, and I don't think I was present with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So you parted ways after Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So this last segment, then, is not something that you had seen or been present for, this last two minutes?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am going to be moving to have this tape introduced into evidence, Your Honour, up until the beginning of that last segment, which is 1 hour, 10 minutes, and 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit -- yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning this entire document, I have an objection just to one segment. I don't object to any other being admitted. That's 13 minutes 18 seconds, up to 15 minutes and 53 seconds. If you remember, that's the telephone call the witness was asked about yesterday. I believe Madam Bolton, in view of the answers given by the witness concerning that part of the video footage, has not established enough link between the witness and that evidence and did not meet the requirements of point 27 of your guidelines. The witness said he had no recollection, and the call made by General Mladic himself is not sufficient, I think, for this to be admitted into evidence. I don't mind this segment being MFI'd and perhaps being introduced through another witness, but I would object to it being admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Guideline 27 indicates that: "Where one of the parties seeks the admission of a document through a witness, it must demonstrate to the Trial Chamber the relation between the witness and the document." Obviously we're not dealing with a document here. I think the issue is one of whether you can be satisfied this is authentic. With respect to that, I would suggest that there are -- would I remind you of guideline 31, which -- and Rule 89, that the general rule is that you may admit any relevant evidence that you deem to have probative value, and I'd suggest that there is a presumption in essence in favour of admissibility. What we are seeking to introduce is a video-tape that we played in continuous form, and the witness has established a relationship to all the segments of the video except the last segment that we're not seeking to tender, and the radio segment. He has, in this case -- the witness has recognised all the footage that came before the radio -- or, sorry, the telephone call, as well as the footage that came afterwards. In addition, there are what I would call circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness found in the call in the footage itself, in particular what I'm referring to is that the subject matter of the telephone conversation is referenced in the initial conversation that this witness was present for in the boardroom. So what General Mladic says in the boardroom - and we can find this in the transcript of this tape which is 65 ter, I think, 9057.01. If I could have that document brought up. Sorry, 9597.01. Could we have page 3, please. You will see there, Your Honours, at lines 6 and 7 that General Mladic indicates: "I'm going to see what the Serbs have been doing at Zepa." This then ties in -- oh, sorry. And he's also, as we've indicated during questioning of this witness -- sorry, if we could then go to page -- the transcript of the portion of the actual call, which we find at page 8. It starts at 7, but I'm interested in page 8. You'll see that there is in fact, discussion in that phone conversation, or he has obtained in that phone conversation some information about Zepa, because then he's talking about how they're pounding in two stages there: "Zepa, Zepa, let's go" -- or, "let us go." So there clearly is a tie between the initial boardroom footage where he says he's going to check on what's happening in Zepa and the subsequent conversation that actually takes place which is one circumstantial guarantee of trustworthiness. The other circumstantial guarantee of trustworthiness is the fact that the footage which a runs continuously on the tape all has -- bears the same date, being the 18th of July. So bearing in mind the standard of admissibility before this Court, we certainly feel that we have met the threshold for admissibility. And any issue my friend has with respect to the fact that the witness wasn't -- or sure if he was present during that part of the conversation is something that goes to the weight and not the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. I did not challenge authenticity nor the right of the Chamber to admit any evidence according to Rule 29. I just invoked your guidelines and said that through this witness who doesn't know anything about it, this document should not be admitted. Mrs. Bolton gave up on tendering the last segment when she realised this witness didn't know anything about it. The same principle applies. We cannot introduce through a witness something that the witness knows nothing about according to your own guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we take a break and come back at half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, how much longer are you still going to be with this witness? I'm sorry to have to ask you this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I anticipate five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We had left, Your Honour, with the issue of the -- my seeking to tender the video-tape into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I saw the difference between what the witness said about the telephone and what he says about the last part of the tape is that he's certainly sure that he was not there with respect to the last part. But the first part he says he's not -- he doesn't ... Is this a question of weight?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Ms. Bolton asked the witness yesterday whether he remembered that phone conversation, and I think he answered no, and that's how I interpreted it. If she did not ask him -- and let us create a fair situation here, and why don't we play it this way: If -- I'll try to be fair during my cross-examination, and then you can decide about the objection. I don't want to go into this before in front of the witness. But I didn't understand him to have said that he has any knowledge at all about the document, and that's my problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why can't we go to the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the -- it's on page 56 of the draft version, line 14. The question at line 16, the reply: [In English] "Were you present when that phone call that we watched earlier was made?" Answer: --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 56 of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the provisional version of the -- the unrevised version of the transcript. I don't know what the official version is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. Line 14 is question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. "And were you present when that phone call that we watched earlier was made?" "I don't remember was I present or not, and I just saw that on the screen, but I -- and -- but I don't remember that I was present." Sure. Now, he has answered that he doesn't remember a lot of things that he's been asked today about incidents that he -- he knew some parts of. And this is precisely what I'm saying to you, that on the last bit of the tape today that Madam Bolton withdrew from tendering, he says clearly, "I was not there. I'd gone to visit my cousin." And yet many other parts of the tape he's been asked questions, "Do you remember this?" "No, I don't." "Do you remember when you spoke to Mr. Perisic the first time?" "No, I don't remember." "Did you see how he came?" "No, I don't." That doesn't invalidate the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm not saying that it invalidates the tape, but if the witness say that he is unfamiliar with something, I believe it isn't sufficient grounds for tendering the document in that way. He doesn't remember. Anything that could establish a link between this witness and a document. He spoke about other things as not remembering them, but the video-tape reminded him. But this segment, I understood him to say that he remembers nothing at all. Then how can a link between the witness and the document be established without the witness even being in the document? I don't want to go into this discussion to deeply, Your Honours, and I know your preference of -- for simple explanations. So I'm simply saying that no link has been established between this part of the video footage and this witness in line with Rule 28 of the guidelines. And about that other segment, he said even more, that he believed the place there to be Gorazde. Sorry, it's guideline 27, to avoid misunderstandings. Yes, it's 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're standing up, Madam Bolton. I was seeing you, but I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt your train of thought, Your Honour, but there was one argument that I failed to mention before lunch, which was that during cross-examination -- or sorry, during examination of the witness at page 9519, you may recall that I read to him a portion of the signed statement he gave to the Prosecution in September 2009, in which case he did authenticate that portion of the video. So having -- up until Mr. Lukic raised the issue and started saying things in court like, "I know the witness wasn't there," the witness was saying he could authenticate it. So my respectful submission is out-of-court statement is more reliable on this issue that his I-don't-remember-today statement. And again it's the entire video we're seeking to tender, not parsing it up into little clips. It's a continuous video that more than established the relationship between the witness and the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you pass me again what is it he authenticated?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is a portion of his written statement where it says as follows: "During the September 8th interview, I was shown footage," and I'm reading from page 9519 of the transcript, ERN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that yesterday's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately mine is still --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Oh, still provisional? Oh, okay. It would be approximately 12 pages from the end of yesterday's transcript. The start of the page would say: "MS. BOLTON: Yes, thank you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what the page that says?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The top -- well, I suppose it's also possible that my page divisions are different than yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do have a "Miss Bolton: Yes, sir. Now you have had an opportunity to watch" -- okay. That's not it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No. I think it's -- if you go back two pages from that, Your Honour. Top of the page may say, "Yes, thank you." And around line 7 on my copy it says, "During the September 8 interview."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So this was me reading to him from his typed statement. "During the September 8 interview, I was shown footage ERN," and this is the same ERN as the tape we have been dealing with, approximately 1 minute and 6 seconds to 15 minutes and 51 seconds. And the footage in question is encompassed in that time period. And he said then: "It was taken in the VMA hospital boardroom on July 16th, 1995." Then he talks about who was present. And then he says at the end: "I can confirm that this footage is authentic." Then in court he was simply saying he couldn't remember he was there or not. So that's a further piece of evidence I'd ask Your Honour to consider in your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I guess your hands say it all, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted to say that I wasn't going to reply, but I do stand by my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Overruled, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could the tape then be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please, it may. 9597.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exactly. 65 ter document 9597 will be given Exhibit P2806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, that's from 1 minute to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1 hour, 10 minutes, 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct. And I would also ask Your Honour that the transcript of that tape which is 9597.01 be admitted into evidence, and I'm just going to locate the start of that last conversation that we're not relying on. I believe if the first 32 pages of that transcript -- wait. Yes. If the first 32 pages were admitted and not pages 33 and 34 in English, that would cover -- oh, no, I'm sorry. I don't think, actually, the transcript includes that last portion of conversation, Your Honour, so I think we could file the transcript in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And the transcript is 9597.01. It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2807. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I have just a couple more questions for you. When we were talking yesterday at page 9.489 of the transcript, we were talking about whether you'd had any contact with either politicians or military leaders from the RS outside of the Balkans, and you told us once you had in New York. And I'd just like you to identify for me, please, a couple of photographs. I think the first one is 65 ter 9600.08. Sir, do you recognise the photo that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were you present when that photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where was that taken?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you know what Mr. Lesic has in his hands?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had a -- some photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shouldn't the witness first tell us who the people are?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The gentleman who has the object in his hand is whom?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay, and the gentleman whose hand he's shaking?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who is the other gentleman in the photo?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nebojsa Govedarica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you spell that, please.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: G-o-v-e-d-a-r-i-c-a.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where is that gentleman from, what country?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of -- of what year this photo was taken in?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If that could be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I challenge the relevance of this exhibit and this part of the evidence concerning the meeting in New York. I don't believe that my learned friend has demonstrated that this is in any way relevant to this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The only relevance would be to establishing the nature of the relationship between the witness and leadership of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except that the witness is not in the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, but he's indicated he was present when it was taken, Your Honour, in New York on this trip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled. It will be admitted into evidence. Have you asked it to be admitted, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2808.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if I could have 65 ter 9600.06.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the three gentlemen in this photo, sir?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who are they?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ned Krayishnik, Dr. President Radovan Karadzic, and Mr. Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay, and where was this was photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you have any recollection of the year?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, I believe it was 1994, but I'm not sure. I don't have any diary on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what were you doing in New York?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to -- there was, I believe, a meeting at the UN, and we tried that we were going to be able to attend at UN to observe, and we were not able to, so we met him at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir. Finally --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2809. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could bring back up Exhibit P2803, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You recall, this photo we discussed earlier, sir. Could you tell me where Mr. Lesic was when this photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We have seen video-tape in these proceedings from events of July 16th, July 17th, some footage from -- of car parts being exchanged on July 18th, and later footage in Pale with Dr. Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik. Could you tell me, did anybody video-tape this meeting at the picnic area on July 18th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, definitely somebody was, because there's pictures there, and as I see also, Mr. Ilija Rakanovic holding a camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was did somebody video-tape, not take photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that there was, but I'm not sure who did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that video-tape, sir?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you know who would?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anybody, I don't know. I would be again guessing. And maybe Mr. Lesic, maybe not. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever seen the tape of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until you showed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, the tape of -- a video-tape of the actual meeting with Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Two last questions, sir. Without telling anybody who you work for, what is the nature of the work that you do now?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am an insurance broker.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in the -- in that position are you required to read documentation like contracts?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Policies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I have nothing further. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krayishnik, good afternoon. I will address you in Serbian, and I leave it to you to choose the language in which you want to reply. If you choose to reply in Serbian, I have two remarks: Please wait a moment after my question for the interpreters to be able to interpret into English. And we'll also have the court usher to change your channel into Serbian, because otherwise you will have another voice in your headphones. But if you want to reply in English, I haven't -- I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can see that you started speaking to me in Serbian, and I suppose that you will continue that way.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you can no longer hear the English interpretation. You only can hear me in Serbian. That will make communication easier.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first interview you had with Ms. Bolton, she asked you that on the 9th of August this year, you said the interview was taped as far as you remember and later transcribed, and you had the chance to read it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second interview that was made after about a month, took place on the 8th of September, 2009. It's recorded as such, and it -- you don't remember whether it was taped too?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it was. I'm not certain though, because I remember more easily what happened 15 or 20 years ago than what happened two weeks ago or a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the note about that second interview, as Ms. Bolton reminded you, you signed two days later, on the 10th of September?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She -- she brought it, and I read my statement and signed -- my statements, correction, and I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously there are differences in the two interviews, because the first one shows clearly that an entire transcript was made with questions and answers, whereas the second document appears like your statement.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please do wait a moment after my question. Did you happen to ask Ms. Bolton whether there is an entire transcript of your second interview with her, with both questions and answers when you signed it or later?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that she brought it and gave -- gave it to me to read at our third meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I do have an objection to raise, but I don't wish to put -- I don't wish the witness to be present when I make the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Krayishnik, do you think you can step out for a short while. It looks like they want to gossip about you. Don't go far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry about that, Your Honour. My objection is that my friend has to have a good-faith basis for the question that he's asking, and we have disclosed to him the notes of the RCMP officer who was present during the interview where he clearly states that Mr. Krajisnik was given the option of having the interview recorded or are preparing a proofing note at the end, and he declined to have it recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if that is the case. I tried to read a handwritten note, and believe me, it was very difficult for me to read a handwritten text. But I have no reason to doubt Ms. Bolton's words, so I will not question this any further. I can show this handwritten note. It is very difficult to read. It's like a doctor's handwriting. But, okay, I don't have a problem with your -- with it now after your reply, and I will ask questions that go in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that you accept the objection? Upheld. You may call the witness. You may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krayishnik, for obliging. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have some questions about your background. As far as I understand, you left the former Yugoslavia as -- for political reasons, as it were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that your father had been a royalist. For this Trial Chamber to understand it better, you meant to say that he was a supporter of the royal house of Karadjordjevic, and the rule of the Karadjordjevic dynasty and pre-war Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I also understood that you are an anti-Communist by conviction, if I may say that.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the interview -- interview that you gave to the OTP, I also understood that you are a deeply religious man and a follower of the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not consider myself deeply religious, but I do think that I'm a faithful man and a Christian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's something else that follows from your interview, but to avoid any misunderstanding on the point of the Trial Chamber, you are not in any way related to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you didn't know him before the -- these encounters which you testified about with reference to the year 1992 and the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, I never met him or knew him until I came to visit in 1992 with humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your personal desire to help the Serbian people in Bosnia came to life after war broke out, and you didn't give any material or financial aid to the Serbian leadership in Bosnia before the war started in something -- anything like lobbying for anybody to come to power or anything?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I right -- or, rather, let me ask you first. Did you follow the changes in power in Bosnia-Herzegovina when at the first multi-party elections Communist rule was overthrown and the ethnic parties came to power jointly?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did follow, and I was glad that the end of a single party system had come. I consider that system to have been a dictatorial one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that sense your sympathy was with the SDS, which was a clearly anti-Communist Party which in its programme wanted to detach itself completely from the early traditions of the Communist movement and had much stronger ties with Orthodox Christianity?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Krayishnik, would you please stop for a short while after the question to allow the interpreters to interpret. Can you also do the same, Mr. Lukic. I could hear they are struggling to keep pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how did you see Slobodan Milosevic and the leadership of the FR Yugoslavia at the time? Did they also want to detach themselves from the old Communist traditions at that time?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier in the news and in the papers there were reports about a multi-party system to be introduced. That socialist system I didn't consider to be democratic, because that socialism, as it was called in Yugoslavia, the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, wasn't anything I believed in, because there was no democracy. There was no multi-party system. And, to us, communism and socialism were the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I may conclude that, according to you, Slobodan Milosevic continued that tradition that existed in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He didn't want to renounce the Red Star, the Communist Party, and Tito, to strike a comparison between him and Karadzic and the parties in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to read a book in which he said that he was a convinced Communist, a member of Skoj, and I concluded from that that he was no different than Tito was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And during those changes in 1992, that is 1991, 1992, especially once things started happening in Bosnia, what was your image of the Yugoslav People's Army and later on the Army of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Was it linked more to the partisan Communist movement or the Chetnik movement which was closer to the royal family of Karadjordjevic?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was too early to make up one's mind at the beginning, but I understood that in those events all Serbs had understood that they had been tricked by communism and that it was -- it was an illusion. And to my mind there was no difference between fascism and communism. I -- it was clear to me that the people had understood that they had been tricked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you under -- agree with me when I say that Ratko Mladic and the -- the VRS started establishing ever-stronger connections with the old traditions and the army from the First World War and started distancing themselves from the Partisan movement and the Communist movement?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When saw pictures of Ratko Mladic in the Krajina, I believe it was at Knin, he disappointed me very much because he had taken the Ustasha coat of arms and the cockade, and he said to me -- rather, not to me. Correction, he said that to him it was the same. And I was greatly disappointed, because he had shown that he didn't understand which system had brought us to the situation that we were in. But later as everybody else, I saw that he began to understand that it was all an illusion and that the entire system was based to harm the Serbian people exclusively and to benefit all other peoples in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later during those encounters that you had in the course of the years personally, did you observe stronger ties with the church?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew a man in Canada who personally during the war was with Ratko Mladic's father. They were members of the movement of the Royal Yugoslav Army. It was Draza Mihajlovic's movement. His father was called Nedjo, and he was -- he fought on the side of the Chetniks through the entire war, and he was killed by the partisans. But I saw statements made by Ratko Mladic that his father was a partisan and was killed by Chetniks. And the colleague of his father heard of -- heard that and called me and informed me of that. He said that he couldn't believe that Ratko Mladic were -- didn't know who killed his father and who his father was siding with. He had photographs showing his father, that gentleman whose name was Savo Mandic, and he gave them to me to bring him the photographs and -- which I did. And when he saw them, he started crying. Tears came to his eyes, and he said that it was hard for him to understand how he had lived so long without knowing who his father had -- had been siding with and how he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had the opportunity in Canada to follow the reporting of various media about the goings on in what's usually here called former Yugoslavia since the war started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me when I say that the Western media reported about the war that broke out in the former Yugoslavia, especially Bosnia-Herzegovina, on -- on practically a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you didn't trust that information. You considered them to be some sort of propaganda, and that's why you wanted to see information that stems from the Serbian side or from RTS by satellite; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then based on the information that you got personally or from your friends or through the Serbian media, you formed an opinion that the Western media were partial and that they favoured the Croatian Muslim sides and the Serbs are to blame for everything; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you also knew in the diaspora that the Croatian and Muslim sides had strong lobbies in those media and that significant funds were invested into creating such an image in the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of your donations, and when I say "yours" I mean the organisation, was to provide hope to the radio television of the Republika Srpska, for them to be able to acquire technical equipment for spreading news about the real struggle of the Serbian people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll pass over to a different topic now. Ms. Bolton didn't ask questions about that, but I may, in the interest of the Defence, ask a few questions about that to hear what you know. As we were able to see, during the period from the end of 1992 till the end of 1995, that is almost throughout the entire war, you were able to go to Bosnia, that is Republika Srpska, several times; correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From what you were able to see and hear in the media, and I believe that you were interested, you were able to tell that there is a great interest in striking some kind of peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we visited, nobody expected the whole thing to last so long. And we emigres were also surprised that this took so long, and we -- we thought that it could all have been shorter and with fewer casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at a certain moment there was this so-called Vance Plan, I believe in 1993, when the Pale leadership refused to accept the plan as proposed, mostly due to the maps, even though Milosevic and Dobrica Cosic and the Greek prime minister all tried to convince the leadership at Pale to accept it? Do you remember that? The media reported about it at length.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You probably know that the Pale leadership and the Serbian people of the Republika Srpska refused the plan of the Contact Group in July 1994, and that after that the leadership of the FRY, I believe it was in early August in 1994, put in place sanctions against the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was an embargo, but I don't remember any commission that were -- that engaged in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you know that a certain moment -- at a certain moment the Yugoslav authorities imposed sanctions on the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we were greatly disappointed, but -- and we thought that it might not be true, but Dr. Srdjan Trifkovic in Chicago, I believe, there was a meeting of some kind. And there he confirmed that it was indeed true, that there was a blockade and sanctions against Republika Srpska imposed by Slobodan Milosevic and that Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your encounters with the Pale leadership or the leadership of the VRS, now you said that you were greatly disappointed by that. Did you ask whether those sanctions are real, whether the blockade was really in place, and whether they were really suffering from having no communication with Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that Dr. Trifkovic was some sort of liaison between the Government of Republika Srpska and the diaspora, and he really convinced that it was real, that it was no fairy tale but it was really so in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The questions I've put to you so far were so-called background questions, and now I'm moving on to specific events. You've come here to give evidence about what you remember concerning particular facts. You said a moment ago, and I believe you've mentioned it in your interview - if you need to see your statement we can give you a reference - that you never kept a diaries or notes on your travels.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time you did not really care about noting down who you met with, what they said about particular things. All you cared about was travelling there and handing over the aid.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Those were long trips. We were usually very tired, and I did not pay much attention to some less important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just make one distinction. Mr. Lesic was the treasurer of your organisation, and he was much more concerned about keeping evidence and recording things, what happened, when. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I don't think he kept notes either, but he did make recordings, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From these tapes I noticed another thing, and I'll ask for your confirmation. Mr. Lesic seems to be impressed in this footage by -- by all these people he's getting to meet, and he's placing himself in the centre, in the limelight.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Bolton asked me about it. He is that sort of person. He likes to be in the first row always. I don't think he's ill-intentioned or a bad person because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not what I meant to say. When Madam Bolton questioned you and when you gave evidence before this Honourable Chamber about these meetings, you remembered all of that mainly on the basis of photographs and video footage, but you don't remember any details.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. These photographs have helped me the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Obviously my friend is entitled to lead when he's asking questions of the witness, but he keeps -- he keeps on occasion giving his own observations as well in the questions, and I don't think that's appropriate, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Give an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "From these tapes I noticed another thing ..." this is lines 9 and 10 of page 77. And we also have a lot of compound questions. So I rise just to ask my friend if he could keep his questions one at a time and not include his own observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You also take your objections one at a time. Let's deal with them one at a time. "From these tapes I noticed other thing and I'll ask you for your confirmation." And then he goes ahead and asks for his confirmation. Obviously he can only ask him about what he know, what he observes, and either what he perceives through his senses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I did not give, probably, the best example, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Until you give me a better example --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- then we'll strike that one off. The other one you say is asking compound questions. Example?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, lines 16 to 19 he's put two propositions to him. One is that: "You remembered all of that mainly on the basis of photographs and video footage," and then he puts a second proposition that he doesn't remember any details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On this question of compound questions, it seems to be a speciality in the Tribunal to ask compound questions. I have yet to come against -- across anyone who asks one fact at a time. And I can tell you that he's going tell you -- yeah. And the one is the flip side of that, you remember from footage and photographs, but on your own you don't remember. You know, I really don't know how to rule on that one, because that has been my frustration with questions here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, I understand, Your Honour. I know the guidelines say we're to avoid complicated and compound questions and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know. I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- I just wished the Chamber to remind Mr. Lukic that have guideline and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I remind everybody, Madam Bolton included, to ask a question containing one fact at a time. And my training says if your sentence goes more than eight words, you're beginning to go into a compound question. "What's your name?" "Where do you come from?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just giving examples. "What's your father's name?" That's the kind of question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up P2792.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave evidence about this photograph yesterday, Mr. Krayishnik. This is October 1993. It's the same location, if I'm not mistaken, as the location of the other photographs you recognised as dating from 18 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see the table is set. We can see glasses and bottles. The plates are not very well -- very clear on the photograph, but we have a hard copy. Do you remember was there luncheon?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this photograph, that's what I'm asking. Do you remember that then, in 1993, a luncheon was organised there?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you remember that because you saw the table set on the photograph; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm looking at the print version of this photograph, and my friend has suggested that the table is set, and I disagree. I see no plates. I can show my friend the blow-up and -- I think perhaps the Chamber needs to see the blow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you -- if you disagree -- I'm not quite sure -- are you just standing up to say you are disagreeing?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I'm saying I think the question is unfair because it suggests that the table is set, and in fact the photograph shows the table is not set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to speed things up, but it looks like I'm not going to be able to. Let us show V000-2816 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. You see when, an objection is raised, the Chamber must rule on that objection before we go to the next point. So you don't sort of dodge it by saying, Okay, let's go to the next thing. When I said, "Mr. Lukic," I wanted you to respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] right. On this photograph I cannot see any plates. I cannot be sure about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection upheld. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the witness has just answered, but let us show video footage V000 -- sorry, it's 65 ter 9599, the very beginning of the clip. It might just assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. The first -- the first few seconds of this footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which footage is this, 9599?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The one that was shown by Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Something else. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is helping us with this. Will they be able to help us maybe? [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think -- is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So from 0:00:00 to 00:21, does this remind you that a luncheon was organised as well on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you first talked to Mrs. Bolton in August 2009, you did not have the opportunity then to see any photographs or videos. You were trying then to answer her questions to the best of your recollection; correct?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a recording of our conversation at the hotel. The weather was very bad with a lot of thunder and rain, and as you can see in the transcript, there are many corrections of spelling and names and place names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is that on that occasion she did not show you any photographs or video-clips. She just asked you to cast your mind back and try to remember things.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those questions related to the period of 14 to 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourteen to 17 years ago. The period from 1992 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the second interview, after reviewing photographs and video footage that Mrs. Bolton used to refresh your memory, you made certain corrections and additions to what you had said the first time.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to remember on my first meetings there were two or three photographs that Mr. Lesic had given me, but very few photographs, just two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that first interview, and if necessary we can show it to you, you said you thought you went to that trip with Mr. Salapura and then you refreshed your memory with photographs and videos, and then you corrected yourself and said it was not the time when you went with Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in the first interview you believed it was the trip you made with Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I thought so at the time, but I wasn't sure. Then in the second interview, I had already realised that he had not been with us that time. It was another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, in the first interview when the Prosecutor asked you about Mr. Perisic, you said you had not talked to him on that occasion, and then -- and you said you were sitting at the other end of the table with your back to him, and then in the second interview after again reviewing documents, you said that you did have a conversation with him; right?

utterances.speaker: NED KRAYISHNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think my friend is -- should be using the actual transcript. A part of what he said I agree with, but part of what he said is not accurate to my recollection of -- of what was said in the -- in the first audio-taped interview. So if he could take us to the pages of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you take us to the pages of the transcript, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if it assists my friend, I don't disagree that he did not recall having any conversation with General Perisic, but I don't recall the reference about him sitting at the other end of the table with his back to him. It was something else he said, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we please see 1D04-0476, page English 22, Serbian 15. Sorry, no. B/C/S is also 22. No, B/C/S is 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you are going to come back to this video-tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. No, Your Honour. You're right. I'm not going to show the video-tape. I'm just going to tender this particular clip. I just wanted to show that there was a luncheon organised, because that was not obvious from the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When I say you're going to come back to that video-clip, for purposes of tendering or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now we are on what, 04-0476. Does it -- is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Point us to the paragraph, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me find it. We would also need to see it, next page. We're reading from line 21. The Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read from page 15 in B/C/S. I'll read from line 22 on. In English it's line 25 in English. So in Serbian it reads: "Did you talk to him a lot?" Your answer is: "No. In fact, I didn't talk to him at all. They were talking. They were sitting, and they were able to -- Ratko and all these important officers" --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What I have on my screen isn't corresponding with what my friend is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Neither is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. We'll have to find the right page in English. Can we turn the page in English? Your Honours, may I have your permission to adjourn for today, and we'll find all this for the start of our first session tomorrow. It will be easier to organise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do adjourn --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do adjourn, I am aware that you've just begun your cross-examination. Are you able to say how long you're going to be with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think I can. I think I'll take less than one session. Certainly less than one session. Up to one hour. Perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The reason I am raising this point, Mr. Harmon, tomorrow is the fifth day we will -- fifth consecutive day we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge David is only coming back on -- in the night of the 6th -- on the night of the 6th. I'm not sure when the next witness is coming. I know he's coming from Canada, and I'm not sure whether -- when he's scheduled to be testifying. If he's scheduled to be testifying sometime this week after tomorrow, we can't sit because we will have sat five days on Friday, and Judge David won't be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is currently scheduled to testify on Friday. He hasn't left Canada yet. We can resolve the issue of his departure from Canada, and we will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hence my raising the point. I thought there might just be a chance we can resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are most welcome. Okay. Unfortunately, Mr. Krayishnik, we've got to give this court to another case that must sit now. We have got to stop at this time. We're not done with you yet. We will have you come back again tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the morning. Same courtroom. Once again, no discussion with anybody about the case during that interval. See you tomorrow morning. Court adjourned until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
